summary.one_line: An Ahmedabad hardware system integrator for Gujarat and Maharashtra government schools and PSUs, now pivoting to solar EPC. It is raising a Rs.300 crore fresh issue, mainly to park as fixed deposits behind bank guarantees. The business has thin margins, heavy working capital and no visible moat, and there are several governance flags.
bull_points: Entirely fresh issue of Rs.300 crore with no offer for sale, so all the money goes to the company and the promoters sell nothing (S2, S3).
Revenue from operations rose from Rs.1,020.57 crore in FY24 to Rs.1,396.63 crore in FY26, and PAT recovered to Rs.45.47 crore in FY26 from Rs.41.67 crore in FY25 (S5, S9).
The order book reached about Rs.2,663 crore by June 2026, roughly 1.9x FY26 revenue, which gives multi-year revenue visibility if it is executed (S9, S11).
Long record of delivering large state digitisation projects, such as 7,500 ICT labs and the Gyankunj school digitisation programme in Gujarat, plus the e-Gram Vishwagram manpower contract (S1).
bear_points: Gross margin fell from 13.04% (FY23) to 9.45% (FY24) to 6.77% (FY25), and the PAT margin is only 3.26% in FY26. This is the economics of an L1-bid hardware reseller, not an IT services firm (S1, S5).

Rs.155 crore of the proceeds goes into fixed deposits pledged for performance bank guarantees, not into productive assets. The company itself says it lacks enough identified projects to be sure of using this money (S1).
Borrowings rose 3.6x in one year, from Rs.48.10 crore to Rs.174.36 crore (FY26). Cumulative FY24-26 operating cash flow of about Rs.50 crore compares with Rs.137 crore of PAT (S1, S2, S10).
About 88% of the order book is now renewable energy, where management admits limited experience. FY26 renewable EPC revenue of Rs.124.70 crore carried costs of Rs.119.63 crore (S1, S7, S9).

The group company Arrow Powertech, where the MD is a director, is both a supplier (Rs.20.47 crore of purchases) and a customer (Rs.17.92 crore of revenue) in FY25. The RHP also shows gaps of up to Rs.48.60 crore between lender stock statements and the books (S1, S6).
watch_points: Whether the Rs.155 crore of guarantee FDs actually turns into new contract wins. Bid success rate fell from 30.91% in FY24 to 19.48% in FY26 (S1, S5).
Execution and margin on the Khavda 272 MWp solar contracts and the PM-KUSUM projects, which make up most of the order book (S1, S9).
Receivable days (171 in FY26) and the debt trajectory. The company's own FY27 working-capital plan assumes Rs.400 crore of borrowings (S1, S10).
Final subscription on 25 September. Day-1 demand was only 0.57x overall, and the anchor book came entirely from four AIFs with no mutual funds or insurers (S13, S16).

reasoning: The money does not build a better business. About 52% of the Rs.300 crore (Rs.155 crore) becomes fixed-deposit collateral so the company can issue bank guarantees, and another Rs.60 crore funds working capital (S1, S2). The IPO mostly replaces collateral that a supplier's (Acer's) bankers and promoter guarantees used to provide (S1). It adds no capacity, technology or pricing power.

There is no moat. Government work is won as the L1 lowest bidder, against Dynacons, Team Computers, L&T, Hitachi Systems Micro Clinic and others (S1). Gross margin has roughly halved to 6.77% in three years (S1), 77.96% of purchases come from three technology partners (S1), and the bid success rate has dropped to 19.48% (S5). This is a box-moving integrator whose edge is its Gujarat tender track record, which is not durable.

The growth story has changed without proof. About 88% of the order book is now solar EPC and PPA work (S9), a segment the DRHP admits management has limited experience in (S1). The first year of it earned about a 4% gross margin: Rs.124.70 crore of revenue against Rs.119.63 crore of cost (S7). Investors would be paying for an EPC contractor with no track record.

Cash quality and leverage are weak. Cumulative FY24-26 operating cash flow of about Rs.50 crore is roughly a third of cumulative PAT of Rs.137 crore (S1, S10). Debt jumped from Rs.48.10 crore to Rs.174.36 crore in FY26 (S2). The company's own FY27 plan needs Rs.400 crore of borrowings on top of the IPO money to fund Rs.640 crore of net working capital (S1).

Governance needs more comfort than the documents give. The group company Arrow Powertech (the MD sits on its board) is both a material supplier and a customer, yet the DRHP says there are no common pursuits (S1). The RHP reports lender stock-statement variances of up to Rs.48.60 crore and an unregistered IREDA charge (S6). There are also recurring promoter loans, offices leased from promoters, and statutory-due and CSR slippages (S1).

Concentration adds risk on top of the thin margins. Top-5 clients were 76.66% of FY26 revenue, government/PSU clients 83.84%, and three states over 86% (S5). One lost or delayed state programme could wipe out a year's profit, given a 3.26% net margin (S5).

subsections.title: What ArMee actually does and how it earns revenue

blocks.text: ArMee began as a partnership firm, M/s Armee Infotech, run by Kiritkumar Patel and Ami Patel from 2003. It was folded into the current company, originally incorporated in 2011 as Blossom Infraspace, from April 2017, and converted to a public company in 2024 (S1). It describes itself as an IT infrastructure and IT managed services company that has also entered retail through Acer Experience Zones and solar EPC/PPA development (S1).

In practice the core business is supplying and installing hardware for government digitisation programmes. It buys computers, interactive panels, tablets and servers from OEMs, installs them in classrooms, ICT labs and fair-price shops, and maintains them for 3-5 years under the contract (S1). In FY25, IT Infrastructure was 93.22% of revenue (Rs.1,224.32 crore) and IT Managed Services, mainly technical manpower and training, was 6.78% (Rs.89.00 crore) (S1). In FY26 the RHP splits revenue into IT infrastructure solutions (Rs.628.20 crore), traded goods (Rs.570.29 crore), IT managed services (Rs.73.25 crore) and renewable EPC (Rs.124.70 crore) (S7). About 41% of revenue is therefore plain traded goods.

blocks.caption: Revenue mix by segment (Rs. crore; FY24-25 from DRHP, FY26 from RHP via secondary source)
rows: IT Infrastructure (incl. traded goods in FY24-25)

blocks.text: Pricing is contract-based. Government jobs are won by tender and awarded to the lowest (L1) bidder, then billed on milestones (S1). Under BOO/BOOT contracts, such as ICT labs in 679 Bihar schools, ArMee funds the hardware up front and recovers the cost over the contract life (S1). The DRHP shows a project value of Rs.385.15 crore for the 7,500-lab Gujarat ICT project and Rs.205.06 crore for the e-Gram Vishwagram manpower contract covering 1,579 executives across 14,179 panchayats (S1).
Read ArMee as a low-margin hardware integrator and trader that depends on state tenders, not as an 'IT services' company. FY25 gross margin was 6.77% (S1).

Customer concentration is extreme and changes from year to year. The single largest client was 70.41% of FY24 revenue (Rs.718.61 crore) and 33.44% in FY25, and the top five clients were 87.63% and 74.04% respectively (S1). In FY26 the top five were 76.66% and government/PSU clients 83.84% (S5). ArMee asked its top five clients for consent to be named in the DRHP and received none (S1).

blocks.caption: Concentration metrics
rows: Top-3 technology partners share of purchases

blocks.text: Geographically, Gujarat was 86.49% of FY24 revenue. In FY25 the mix shifted to Maharashtra (37.04%), Gujarat (36.25%) and Uttar Pradesh (23.33%) (S1). In FY26 Gujarat, Maharashtra and Tamil Nadu together made up 86.48% (S3). Supply is similarly concentrated: the top three technology partners supplied 77.96% of FY25 purchases, with no long-term supply contracts (S1). Acer is clearly a key partner. It appears in project descriptions (20,000 Acer tablets, 235 Acer laptops), its bankers advanced PBG limits for ArMee in FY23-24, and ArMee is Acer's exclusive partner for up to 60 single-brand Experience Zones (S1).
Both ends of the business are concentrated: a handful of state buyers on one side and three OEMs on the other, with ArMee earning a thin spread in between (S1, S5).

subsections.title: Operating model, scale and the solar pivot

blocks.text: ArMee has no factory. It runs from a leased 1,800 sq ft head office in Ahmedabad (leased from the MD), branch offices in Gurugram and Mumbai, a 7,500 sq ft leased godown and third-party warehouses (S1). The workflow runs: tender, PBG submission, procurement from OEMs, delivery and installation, invoicing, then O&M during the warranty period (S1). As of August 2025, 1,630 of its 1,688 payroll staff sat in project implementation, plus 693 contract workers (S1). By June 2026 it reported 263 permanent and 1,648 contractual staff across 99 ongoing projects (S2).

The business mix is changing quickly. In August 2025, renewable EPC made up 68.19% of the Rs.1,915.27 crore standalone order book and solar PPA 19.92% (S1). The largest EPC contracts are three packages for a 272 MWp PV plant at Khavda, Gujarat (cables, balance of system and modules), worth Rs.802.29 crore combined (S1). There are also PM-KUSUM feeder-solarisation projects in Maharashtra and UP, and ArMee is the developer and owner on some of them through SPVs (S1). By June 2026 the order book was about Rs.2,663 crore, 88.38% of it renewable (S9), and the company had 10 EPC, 1 PPA and 2 BESS projects in progress (S5).
Most of what an investor is buying from here is a solar EPC contractor with one year of revenue history. The IT business alone does not explain the order book (S1, S9).

The company-paid D&B report in the DRHP puts India's total IT spending at USD 138.9 billion in 2024 (projected), up 13.2%. Devices are the largest segment at USD 55.8 billion (40.2%), and IT services are USD 26.1 billion (S1). The directly relevant market, state-funded school and e-governance hardware rollouts, is not sized separately. It depends on individual state budgets and central schemes such as Samagra Shiksha, which the company names as schemes it has worked under (S1).

On solar, the D&B report says installed capacity grew from 35.6 GW in FY20 to 105.6 GW in FY25, and cites a target of about 280 GW by 2030 (S1). This is a real tailwind, but it is equally available to hundreds of established EPC contractors.

items: India IT spending 2024P: USD 138.9 billion, +13.2% (Gartner via D&B) (S1)
Devices segment: USD 55.8 billion; IT services: USD 26.1 billion (S1)
Solar installed capacity FY25: 105.6 GW; 24% CAGR since FY20 (S1)

blocks.text: The DRHP names Dynacons Systems & Solutions (listed), Team Computers, Larsen & Toubro, Hitachi Systems Micro Clinic, Value Point Systems and Aabasoft Technologies as key competitors, and acknowledges that several are much larger with economies of scale (S1). For solar EPC it names no competitors, although the field is crowded with specialist EPC firms and developers.
Competition is on price. The company's own process chart shows contracts go to the L1 bidder after technical qualification (S1). Its bid success rate fell from 30.91% in FY24 to 19.48% in FY26 (S5).

blocks.caption: Competitive positioning (from DRHP disclosures)
rows: Resells OEM hardware; top-3 partners 78% of purchases
Track record of large Gujarat education projects; ISO 27001/20000 certifications

blocks.text: No. The DRHP makes no import-substitution, market-share or 'only Indian maker' claim, and there is no licence or regulatory barrier that competitors lack. The real advantages are pre-qualification credentials from past large Gujarat projects and working relationships with state education and panchayat departments (S1). Those help it get onto bid lists, but they do not win bids, which go to the lowest price. The falling gross margin (13.04% to 6.77% over FY23-25) is what a business without pricing power looks like (S1).

The company's main constraint is balance-sheet capacity to post bank guarantees, not capability. That is why the largest use of IPO money is guarantee collateral (S1). Balance-sheet capacity is a commodity that any competitor with capital can match.
Verdict on moat: none demonstrated. Relationships and tender credentials exist, but pricing is set by L1 bidding and supply is controlled by OEMs (S1, S5).

blocks.caption: Restated consolidated financials (Rs. crore). FY24-25 from the DRHP; FY26 from the RHP as reported by secondary sources.

blocks.text: Revenue roughly doubled in FY24 on one very large Gujarat client, which was 70% of that year's revenue. Growth then slowed to 28.7% in FY25 and 6.3% in FY26 (S1, S5). Profit has not kept pace: FY26 PAT of Rs.45.47 crore is still below FY24's Rs.50.13 crore despite 37% more revenue (S3, S5). Management says the drop reflects expansion spending and higher provisions (S11). Figures: S1 for FY24-25; S2, S5 and S9 for FY26.

Return ratios look high (FY26 ROE 28.52%, ROCE 24.10%) because the equity base is small relative to a trading-type turnover. They have also fallen sharply, with ROCE at 57.55% in FY24 and 32.43% in FY25 (S1, S2, S11).

subsections.title: Balance sheet, working capital and cash flow

blocks.caption: Balance sheet and cash flow (Rs. crore)

blocks.text: Operating cash flow of about Rs.49.7 crore over FY24-26 compares with cumulative PAT of Rs.137.3 crore, so only about 36% of profit turned into cash (S1, S10). The FY25 outflow came from a Rs.330.94 crore increase in trade receivables (S1). Receivables stay near 170 days, matched by about 170 days of payables to suppliers (S1, S10). In effect, OEMs are financing ArMee's government receivables.

Borrowings rose 3.6x in FY26. Of the Rs.174.36 crore, Rs.96.70 crore is non-current, tied to the solar build-out and including IREDA funding, and Rs.77.66 crore is current (S6). Lease liabilities also rose from Rs.1.13 crore to Rs.16.25 crore (S6). The DRHP notes emphasis-of-matter comments in the FY23 audit on overdue receivables and loans and advances (S1).

Red flag: the RHP discloses gaps between quarterly stock/receivable statements filed with banks (IOB, ICICI, Bandhan) and the books, up to Rs.48.60 crore in one quarter. The company attributes these to timing and classification differences (S6). The secondary summary's own table is internally inconsistent, so treat the exact figures with care.

subsections.title: Does the trend support the growth story?

blocks.text: Only partly. Revenue has scaled, but margins have compressed, cash conversion is poor and growth in the core IT business stalled in FY26. Excluding the Rs.124.70 crore of new renewable EPC revenue, FY26 revenue was about Rs.1,271.93 crore, roughly 3% below FY25 (S7). The new growth engine, solar EPC, made a gross margin of about 4% in its first year: Rs.124.70 crore of revenue against Rs.119.63 crore of cost (S7).

The company's own FY27 working-capital plan projects net working capital of Rs.639.96 crore. It is funded by Rs.400 crore of borrowings, Rs.60 crore of IPO money and Rs.179.96 crore of internal accruals, with receivables of Rs.1,446.20 crore (S1). Growing the book therefore depends on a lot more debt. The IPO only partly deleverages the company.
Contingent liabilities were Rs.129.23 crore at March 2026 (S11), mostly bank guarantees. Collateralised guarantees were Rs.74.53 crore (S10).

sections.title: Issue details and objects of the issue

blocks.caption: Key issue terms
rows: Rs.300 crore, 80,00,000 shares, entirely fresh issue; no OFS (S2)
Rs.350-375; 40 shares (Rs.15,000 at the upper end) (S2)
Opens 23 Sep, closes 25 Sep, allotment 28 Sep, listing 30 Sep 2026 on BSE and NSE (S2)
Khandwala Securities, Saffron Capital Advisors / Cameo Corporate Services (S2)

blocks.text: All shares are new, so the whole Rs.300 crore (less issue expenses) goes to the company, and the promoters sell nothing (S2). Promoters' average acquisition cost is Rs.5.63-18.09 per share, much of it from a 5:1 bonus issue in February 2024 (S1). The retail quota is unusually large at 52.5%, compared with the more common 35%, which reflects the 25% QIB cap (S2).
The RHP dated 16 September 2026 is hosted by lead manager Saffron (S18). It exceeded fetch size limits, so FY26 figures here come from secondary summaries of it (see method).

blocks.caption: Objects of the issue (Rs. crore)
rows: FDs as collateral for PBGs/EMDs to bid for new Government/PSU projects
General corporate purposes (capped at 25% of gross proceeds) and issue expenses

blocks.text: The DRHP explains that ArMee has to post performance bank guarantees of 3-10% of project value, usually 5%, at the start of each contract. These stay in place for about five years, and once bank non-fund limits are used up it has to post 100% FD cover (S1). At August 2025 it had Rs.125.40 crore of sanctioned non-fund limits, of which Rs.72.11 crore was used (S1). It projects Rs.257.34 crore of PBGs on Rs.5,826.92 crore of expected order value over FY27-28 (S1). The debt-repayment object was cut from Rs.7.50 crore in the DRHP to Rs.6.50 crore in the RHP (S1, S2).

The DRHP itself says the company does not currently have enough identified projects for which the Rs.155 crore can be fully used through FY28 (S1, Risk Factor 12). It also disclosed that in FY23-24 Acer's bankers advanced PBG limits for ArMee's projects (Rs.27.16 crore and Rs.41.36 crore) against third-party collateral (S1). The IPO money largely replaces that support.

subsections.title: What the use of funds means for investors

blocks.text: No rupee of the issue goes into capacity, technology or acquisitions. Guarantee collateral and working capital are needed to keep a low-margin, capital-hungry bidding model growing. Returns on that money are limited by the 3-5% net margins the model earns (S1, S5).

The deployment is also flexible. The DRHP allows unspent amounts to roll into later years and surpluses to move between objects, and no monitoring agency appraisal of the plan is mentioned beyond statutory requirements (S1).

The promoters are one family. Ami Ridhish Patel (47, Whole-Time Director, 76.19% pre-issue), her father-in-law Kiritkumar Chimanbhai Patel (77, 10.62%, resigned as director in May 2024) and her husband Ridhish Kiritbhai Patel (51, Chairman and MD since February 2024, 5.91%) (S1). Ridhish holds a BSc, joined in 2012 and was previously CEO of the predecessor partnership. Ami holds a BCom and ran HR and admin (S1). Neither brings disclosed experience in solar EPC, which is now most of the order book (S1).

The board has four independent directors, including Sujit Gulati, a former IAS officer and Joint Secretary in the Ministry of Textiles (S1). There was independent-director turnover just before filing: two IDs left in August 2025 and two joined on 6 September 2025 (S1). The MD's pay is Rs.10 lakh a month and the WTD's is Rs.8 lakh a month plus up to 2% of net profit as a bonus (S1). The CFO has been in place only since FY24 (S1). The company has never paid a dividend (S1).

The RPT section goes beyond the usual salaries and rent. The key item is Arrow Powertech Pvt Ltd, the designated group company, on whose board the MD sits (S1). In FY25 ArMee bought Rs.20.47 crore from it and sold Rs.17.92 crore to it. At March 2025 it owed Arrow Rs.23.95 crore and was owed Rs.20.49 crore (S1). Even so, the DRHP says Arrow is not in the same line of business and there are no common pursuits (S1). Two-way trade of this size with a promoter-linked company needs a clear explanation, and the DRHP does not give one.

blocks.caption: Selected related-party transactions (Rs. crore)
rows: Revenue from ArMee Technology Services (then promoter-linked)
Loans from promoters outstanding at year end
Loans given to iLeads Business Advisory LLP (promoter-linked until Nov 2023)

items: ArMee Technology Services, a promoter-influenced entity that generated Rs.14.85 crore of revenue and a Rs.15.92 crore receivable in FY23, was bought from the promoters for Rs.1.85 crore and became a subsidiary in October 2023 (S1).
A receivable of about Rs.1.61 crore sat with Stratacon Business Advisory LLP in FY23-24. The MD left that LLP in July 2025 (S1).
The head office and a second office are leased from the MD and WTD (S1).
Relatives are on the payroll, for example Vihang Pathak at Rs.48.75 lakh in FY25 (S1).
Promoters and relatives had given personal guarantees of Rs.35.77 crore for company borrowings (S1).

blocks.text: Assessment: this is not a routine RPT profile. There is revolving promoter lending, a group company that is both supplier and customer, and a history of receivables and loans parked with promoter-linked LLPs (S1).

items: Delayed PF, ESIC and statutory dues in FY23-25. Pending amounts were small (Rs.1.05 lakh PF in FY25), but the DRHP concedes past delays (S1).
The FY23 CSR obligation was not fully spent, and unspent amounts were transferred late in July 2024 (S1).
FY23 audit emphasis of matter on overdue receivables (Rs.1.79 crore) and loans and advances (Rs.4.59 crore) (S1).
RHP: variances between bank stock statements and the books of up to Rs.48.60 crore, and an IREDA charge not yet registered (S6).
Outstanding litigation against the company at DRHP: 1 criminal case, 5 tax matters and 2 other matters, totalling Rs.1.44 crore. The amounts are not material (S1).
Lead-manager track record: the review site reports that 7 of the merchant bankers' last 9 IPOs closed below issue price. This is secondary data (S11).

blocks.text: No single item is disqualifying. Taken together, they suggest financial controls that have not yet reached listed-company standard (S1, S6).

items: Execution risk in a new business: about 88% of the order book is solar EPC and PPA work (S9), and the DRHP admits management lacks adequate experience in some of these activities (Risk Factor 37) (S1). First-year EPC gross margin was about 4% (S7).
Customer and state concentration: top-5 clients were 76.66% of FY26 revenue, government/PSU 83.84%, and three states over 86% (S5). The top client swung from 70% of revenue to 33% within a year (S1).

Tender dependence: bids are won on lowest price and the success rate fell to 19.48% (S5). Government contracts allow termination without cause, orders can be varied by up to 25%, delay penalties run up to 10% of project value, and the company can be debarred (S1).
Supplier dependence: 77.96% of purchases come from three technology partners with no long-term contracts. Acer is both a key supplier and past provider of guarantee support (S1).

blocks.text: These risks compound each other. A thin 3.26% net margin (S5) leaves little room for a delayed state payment, an invoked guarantee or a cost overrun on a fixed-price solar EPC contract.

items: Working capital and leverage: receivables of about 171 days (S10), borrowings of Rs.174.36 crore (S2), and a FY27 plan that assumes Rs.400 crore of borrowings (S1).
Bank guarantees: Rs.129.23 crore of contingent liabilities at March 2026 (S11). Any invocation hits cash directly (S1).
Use of proceeds is not tied to identified projects: the company says it cannot assure that the Rs.155 crore PBG object will be fully used as planned (S1).
Related parties and controls: two-way trade with Arrow Powertech, promoter loans, and lender stock-statement variances (S1, S6).

blocks.text: The DRHP's remaining 60-plus risk factors (insurance, IP, general macro) are standard boilerplate and are not repeated here.

No management interview or investor call could be found. The only forward-looking statements are in the offer document. The company projects bidding for projects worth Rs.2,931.72 crore in FY27 and Rs.2,895.20 crore in FY28 that would require guarantees (S1). It projects FY27 net working capital of Rs.639.96 crore, with inventory rising to 17 days and receivables falling to 133 days from 170 (S1).

items: Keep bidding for government/PSU work while adding private clients (S1).
Expand beyond Gujarat and Maharashtra (S1).
Move into BESS, payment devices, data migration and STEM/Atal Tinkering Labs (S1). It has since reported 2 BESS projects (S5).
Open up to 60 Acer Experience Zones, although only one (Ahmedabad) was operating at DRHP (S1).

blocks.text: These are management estimates, and the DRHP says so explicitly. The FY27-28 order values are not backed by identified projects (S1, Risk Factor 12).

The order book gives revenue visibility. At about Rs.2,663 crore it is roughly 1.9x FY26 revenue (S9). However, the RHP's remaining-performance-obligation note covers only the IT segments (Rs.357.32 crore), so the renewable pipeline has no comparable audited disclosure (S7). With margins in both the IT and EPC books in the low single digits, strong revenue growth may still translate into modest profit and cash.

The best case is that fresh guarantee capacity lets ArMee win larger state programmes and solar EPC packages, and scale spreads fixed costs. The base case, which is consistent with FY25-26, is revenue growth with flat margins and rising debt.

subsections.title: Anchor book, subscription so far and grey market

blocks.text: On 22 September ArMee allotted 10.65 lakh shares at Rs.375 to four anchors, raising Rs.39.94 crore, only about 12.5% of the issue (S2, S16, S17). The anchors were Abundantia Capital III (Rs.19.94 crore), Vikasa India EIF-I (Rs.10.00 crore), AMITSG Ventures Fund (Rs.5.00 crore) and VBCUBE Ventures (Rs.5.00 crore). All four are alternative investment funds, and no mutual fund or insurer took part (S15, S16). Lock-in: 50% until 28 October 2026 and 50% until 27 December 2026 (S2).

These are day-1 figures only (S13, S14). The report is written on day 2, and no verified day-2 figures were found from a page that could be opened. The issue closes on 25 September and the final numbers may differ materially. The unofficial grey market premium was reported at Rs.55 on 23 September, up from Rs.1-12 in the preceding days (S12), and at Rs.0 on 18 September (S8). This is volatile, unregulated data and is not treated as an investment signal.
The demand signal so far is weak. There is no domestic mutual fund or insurer in the anchor book, and NII and retail were each around half subscribed after day 1 (S13, S16).

method: Primary source: the DRHP dated 26 Sep 2025 (S1), downloaded from the company website and read page by page. Sections read directly: the issue summary, related-party summary, objects of the issue including the PBG and working-capital workings, business, client and supplier concentration, competition, properties, promoters, group company, board, and selected risk factors (1-17), plus part of the D&B industry section. The DRHP covers FY23-FY25. The RHP dated 16 Sep 2026 (S18), which adds FY26 and updates the objects, was located on the lead manager's site but exceeded the fetch size limit and could not be read directly. All FY26 figures therefore come from secondary summaries of the RHP, cross-checked across at least two sources where possible: revenue, PAT, EBITDA, net worth and borrowings (S2, S3, S5, S9); segment split (S7); cash flow and receivable days (S10); lender-statement variances (S6); order book, government share and top-5 share (S5, S9). The S6 variance table is internally inconsistent, so only its headline maximum is used. FY24 and FY25 operating cash flow come from S1. FY26 client-level and supplier-level concentration beyond the top-5 percentage could not be confirmed. IPO Watch's main page (S4) lists wrong promoter names and post-issue shareholding, so it was not relied on for those. Day-2 subscription could not be confirmed from an opened page, so only day-1 data is used. The grey market premium is reported as unofficial and excluded from the verdict. No management interview or earnings call was found, so the forward outlook relies only on offer-document projections. Valuation (P/E, P/B, peer multiples) is deliberately excluded, including figures volunteered by sources.
